A loyal Stalinist who rose through the Soviet hierarchy during the purges, this politician served as Premier of the Soviet Union from 1955 to 1958 — who is he?

A boilermaker before West Point, this U.S. general graduated in 1915 alongside Dwight Eisenhower in "the class the stars fell on" and later became the first chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff — who is he?
Omar Bradley: United States Army general (1893–1981)

At 93, this Cameroonian head of state is the world's oldest sitting president and the second-longest-ruling leader in Africa, having taken power in 1982 after his predecessor's surprise resignation — who is he?
Paul Biya: President of Cameroon since 1982.

After leaving his party in 2021, this Dutch politician founded a new party called New Social Contract, which won 20 seats in the 2023 election, and helped expose the childcare benefits scandal — who is he?
Alfred, Duke of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha
Commander of Iran's Quds Force from 1998 until his assassination by the United States in 2020, he was called the single most powerful operative in the Middle East — who was he?
Historians use this name for the wave of anticlerical violence — killings and church arson — carried out by leftist groups during the Spanish Civil War; what's it called?
Golden age of arcade video games
Red Terror (Spain): Assassinations during the Spanish Civil War.
As Colombia's Minister of Justice, he cracked down on cocaine traffickers until he was assassinated on the orders of a notorious drug baron in 1984 — who was he?
Rodrigo Lara Bonilla: Colombian lawyer and politician (1946-1984)

Using the alias Saitani Umetarō while hunted by shogunate forces, this low-ranking samurai from Tosa negotiated the alliance between rival domains that helped topple the Tokugawa Shogunate — who was he?
Sakamoto Ryōma: Japanese samurai and politician (1836–1867)

Considered history's largest colonial campaign, this 1935–36 conflict saw two hundred thousand invading troops attack without a declaration, retaking a town that symbolized their army's earlier defeat there four decades before. Which conflict?
Second Italo-Ethiopian War: 1935–1936 war between Italy and Ethiopia.
Grandson of a prime minister and the longest-serving PM in his nation's history, this Japanese politician led the Liberal Democratic Party across two stints in office — who was he?
Shinzo Abe: Prime Minister of Japan (2006–2007; 2012–2020)
The only communist state ever to exist in the Arab world, this nation in southern Arabia had its capital at Aden before unifying with its northern neighbor in 1990 — what was it?
South Yemen: 1967–1990 state in Western Asia.
A London School of Economics graduate from a wealthy family, he led Togo from its 1958 election to independence as prime minister and then president, until his 1963 assassination — who was he?

Sylvanus Olympio: President of Togo from 1960 to 1963. After World War II, Olympio became prominent in efforts for independence of Togo and his party won the 1958 election, making him the prime minister of the country.
Founded by Aleister Crowley in the early 1900s, this occult philosophy centers on discovering one's 'True Will' and the maxim 'Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law' — what is it?
Thelema: New religious movement founded by Aleister Crowley.

Elected by Ostrogothic nobles in 541 after his two predecessors were killed for trying to surrender to the Romans, this penultimate Gothic king reversed the tide of the Gothic War and recovered nearly all of Italy by 543 — who was he?
Totila: King of the Ostrogoths from 541 to 552.
Armenia's first Defence Minister, he had just become prime minister in 1999 when he was assassinated that October — who was he?
Vazgen Sargsyan: Armenian military commander, politician (1959–1999)
The youngest member of China's Gang of Four, this politician organized the Shanghai People's Commune before being deposed and sentenced to life imprisonment after Mao's death — who is he?
Wang Hongwen: Chinese politician and activist (1935–1992)
A South Carolina Army National Guard officer who served as first gentleman of South Carolina from 2011 to 2017, he is the husband of a former state governor and UN ambassador—who is he?
William Michael Haley: American businessman and officer (born 1970)

Founded in 2012 by former TV journalist Yair Lapid, this centrist Israeli party placed second with 19 Knesset seats in its debut election and later co-founded the short-lived Blue and White alliance in 2019 — which party?
Yesh Atid: Israeli political party. Yesh Atid (Hebrew: יֵשׁ עָתִיד, lit. 'There is a Future') is a centrist political party in Israel.
Atatürk's right-hand man took his very surname from the site of two battles he commanded — and went on to serve as Turkey's president from 1938 to 1950. Which leader earned a name from a battlefield?
Who among these was born first?
Ivan Pavlov (born 1849) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was born first?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
Who among these was born first?
Havelock Ellis (born 1859) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four began earliest?
Assembly language (founded 1949) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is an astronomer?
Who among these is a mathematician?
Leonhard Euler is a mathematician. Euler has been called a "universal genius" who "was fully equipped with almost unlimited powers of imagination, intellectual gifts and extraordinary memory".
Pick the chemist from these four.
Maud Menten is a chemist. Maud Leonora Menten (March 20, 1879 – July 17, 1960) was a Canadian physician and chemist.
What is the atomic number of Silicon?
Silicon (SILL-ih-kən) is a chemical element; it has symbol Si and atomic number 14.
In what year was Jerry Buss born?
Jerry Buss: Gerald Hatten Buss (January 27, 1933 – February 18, 2013) was an American businessman, investor, chemist, and philanthropist.
In what year was Pierre Curie born?
Pierre Curie (15 May 1859 – 19 April 1906) was a French physicist and chemist, and a pioneer in crystallography and magnetism.
In what year was Kevin Mitnick born?
Kevin Mitnick: Kevin David Mitnick (August 6, 1963 – July 16, 2023) was an American computer security consultant, author, and convicted hacker.
In what year did John von Neumann die?
John von Neumann: During World War II, von Neumann worked on the Manhattan Project.
In what year did C. V. Raman die?
C. V. Raman: This phenomenon, a hitherto unknown type of scattering of light they called modified scattering, was subsequently termed the Raman effect or Raman scattering.
In what year was Euler's formula discovered?
Euler's formula: The formula is still valid if x is a complex number, and is also called Euler's formula in this more general case.
COBOL: CODASYL. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language;) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.
Propofol: Pfizer. Propofol is the active component of an intravenous anesthetic used for induction and maintenance of general anesthesia.
Boxer (dog breed): German Empire. The Boxer is a medium to large, short-haired dog breed of mastiff-type, developed in Germany.
Who is credited with discovering Special relativity?
Special relativity: Albert Einstein. In physics, the special theory of relativity, or simply special relativity, is a scientific theory of the relationship between space and time.
Who is credited with discovering Carbon dioxide?
Carbon dioxide: Jan Baptist van Helmont. Carbon dioxide is a chemical compound with the chemical formula CO2.
Who is credited with discovering Calcium?
Calcium: Humphry Davy. Calcium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ca and atomic number 20.
Made of adenine bonded to a sugar, this RNA building block underlies ATP, the cell's main energy currency, and doubles as an IV treatment for certain cardiac arrhythmias — what is it?
Adenosine (symbol A) is an organic compound that occurs widely in nature in the form of diverse derivatives.
The simplest pnictogen hydride, with the formula NH3, this pungent gas is also a common nitrogenous waste in living things — what is it?
Ammonia is an inorganic chemical compound of nitrogen and hydrogen with the formula NH3.
This Portuguese economist-turned-dictator ruled as head of government from 1932 to 1968, rebranding his authoritarian regime as the corporatist 'New State.' Who is he?
António de Oliveira Salazar (28 April 1889 - 27 July 1970) was a Portuguese dictator, academic, and economist who served as President of the Council of Ministers of Portugal from 1932 to 1968.
Once native to the highland lakes of Xochimilco and Chalco, this neotenic mole salamander keeps its external gills and stays aquatic for life — what is it?
Axolotl (from Classical; Ambystoma mexicanum) is a species of mole salamander.
What yellow-green digestive fluid is produced continuously by the liver but stored and concentrated in the gallbladder until it's needed to break down fats in the small intestine?
Bile (from Latin bilis), also known as gall, is a yellow-green fluid produced by the liver of most vertebrates that aids the digestion of lipids in the small intestine.

Making up only about 2.6 percent of the brain's total weight, this stalk-like structure connects the cerebrum to the spinal cord and regulates critical functions like heart rate and breathing. What is it called?
Brainstem (or brain stem) is the posterior stalk-like part of the brain that connects the cerebrum with the spinal cord.
This biological family includes domestic dogs, wolves, coyotes, foxes, and jackals, found on every continent except Antarctica. What family is it?
Canidae (from Latin, canis, "dog") is a biological family of caniform carnivorans, constituting a clade.
Despite no clinical evidence it treats any disease, this daisy-like plant is a staple in calming herbal tea, beer brewing, and even garden ground cover — what is it?
Chamomile (American English) or camomile (British English; see spelling differences) (or) is the common name for several daisy-like plants of the family Asteraceae.
This neurological disorder strikes one side of the head around the eye and temple, often at the very same hour each day for an 8-to-10-week stretch before vanishing for months — what condition is it?
Cluster headache is a neurological disorder characterized by episodes of severe headaches on one side of the head, typically around the eye and temple, lasting between 15 minutes to three hours.
Which genus of passerine birds, whose Latin name literally means 'raven,' includes about 46 species commonly known as crows, ravens, and rooks?
Corvus is a widely distributed genus of passerine birds ranging from medium-sized to large-sized in the family Corvidae.
Affecting some 280 million people worldwide, this state of low mood saps motivation and the pleasure once taken in activities — what is it?
Depression (mood) is a mental state of low mood and aversion to activity.
Covering everything from a fibrous bone condition to a kidney disorder, this term for abnormal tissue growth is usually precancerous rather than outright malignant — what is it?

Dysplasia is any of various types of abnormal growth or development of cells (microscopic scale) or organs (macroscopic scale), and the abnormal histology or anatomical structure(s) resulting from such growth.
This thin, protective tissue type lines the outer surfaces of organs and the inner surfaces of blood vessels; the skin's outermost layer is a familiar example. What is it?
Epithelium is a thin, continuous, protective layer of cells with little extracellular matrix.

Likely domesticated from the European polecat, with which it can still interbreed, this slender Mustelid pet weighs up to about two kilograms and comes in coats of black, brown or white — which animal?
Ferret (Mustela furo) is a small, domesticated species belonging to the family Mustelidae.
Caused by a loss of blood supply, this type of tissue death most commonly affects the feet and hands and can turn skin red or black. What condition is it?
Gangrene is a type of tissue death caused by a lack of blood supply. If the gangrene is caused by an infectious agent, it may present with a fever or sepsis.
This term describes the overall system of processes, rules, and power structures that sets boundaries of conduct and steers the direction of an organized group — what is it?

Governance is the overall complex system or framework of processes, functions, structures, rules, laws and norms born out of the relationships, interactions, power dynamics and communication within an organized group of individuals.

His synergy with information-theory father Claude Shannon laid foundations for the Information Age, and during WWII he helped build automatic guns that defended London from V-1 flying bombs — who was this Dutch-American control-theory pioneer?
Hendrik Wade Bode (-d,; December 24, 1905 - June 21, 1982) was an American engineer, researcher, inventor, author and scientist, of Dutch ancestry.
This thin piece of mucosal tissue that surrounds or partially covers the vaginal opening takes its name from a Greek word meaning 'thin skin' — name the structure?
Hymen is a thin piece of mucosal tissue that surrounds or partially covers the vaginal opening. It forms part of the vulva and is similar in structure to the vagina.
One of the largest dog breeds in the world, this sighthound was historically used to course game and became the official mascot of a British Guards regiment in 1902. What breed is it?
Irish Wolfhound is a breed of large sighthound that has, by its presence and substantial size, inspired literature, poetry and mythology.
Originally trained as a mathematician, this English economist built the foundation for an entire school of macroeconomic thought that bears his name — who is he?

John Maynard Keynes (KAYNZ; 5 June 1883 - 21 April 1946), was an English economist whose writings are considered the basis for the school of thought known as Keynesian economics, as well as its various offshoots.
Native to southern China but long cultivated in Japan and Southeast Asia, this small fruit closely resembles an orange in color and texture but is only about the size of a large olive — what is it?
Kumquat are a group of small, angiosperm, fruit-bearing trees in the family Rutaceae.

First isolated from linseed oil and named from the Latin words for 'flax' and 'oil,' this omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid is one of the two essential fats humans must get from their diet — which acid?
Linoleic acid (LA) is an organic compound with the formula CH3(CH2)4CH=CHCH2CH=CH(CH2)7COOH.

A chemical element with symbol Mg and atomic number 12, it's a shiny gray metal with low density and high chemical reactivity that readily reacts with air to form a thin passivation oxide coating. What element is this?
Magnesium is a chemical element; it has symbol Mg and atomic number 12. The free metal burns with a brilliant-white light.
Most common on the legs in women and the back in men, this cancer develops from melanin-producing skin cells and, in extremely rare cases, can even arise in the lungs — which cancer?
Melanoma is a type of cancer, typically skin cancer; it develops from the melanin-producing cells known as melanocytes.
This small, subterranean mammal has velvety fur, tiny eyes, and short powerful forelimbs with oversized paws built for constant digging — what animal is it?

It's the inherent character of the universe as a whole — the laws, elements, and phenomena of the physical world, including life itself — even though humans are often spoken of as somehow apart from it. What is it?
Nature is an inherent character or constitution, particularly of the ecosphere or the universe as a whole.

Classified using a measurement of weight divided by the square of height, this medical condition is diagnosed when that figure exceeds 30 and is linked to cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes — what is it?
Obesity is a medical condition, considered a disease by multiple organizations, in which excess body fat has accumulated to such an extent that it can have negative effects on health.

This genus of 70 to 100 frost-tolerant annual, biennial, and perennial species native to temperate Eurasia, Africa, and North America is the type genus of its flowering plant family — what's the genus?
Papaver is a genus of 70-100 species of frost-tolerant annuals, biennials, and perennials native to temperate and cold regions of Eurasia, Africa and North America.
Its Nahuatl-derived name means 'caterpillar cocoon,' and this small, spineless desert cactus native to northern Mexico and south Texas contains the psychoactive alkaloid mescaline — what's the plant?
Peyote is a small, spineless cactus which contains psychoactive alkaloids, particularly mescaline.
This inflammation of the lining around the lungs causes sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing, and is most often triggered by a viral infection — what condition is it?
Pleurisy is inflammation of the membranes that surround the lungs and line the chest cavity (pleurae).
Classified into acute, chronic, and pelvic pain syndrome subtypes, this condition doesn't always match its name's literal meaning of organ swelling — which condition?
Prostatitis is an umbrella term for a variety of medical conditions that incorporate bacterial and non-bacterial origin illnesses in the pelvic region.
Along with his two brothers, this American physician-turned-businessman acquired the pharmaceutical company behind OxyContin, later linked to the U.S. opioid crisis — who is he?
Raymond Sackler (February 16, 1920 - July 17, 2017) was an American physician and businessman.

Named after the naturalist who first documented it, this highly venomous South Asian snake is known for an extremely painful bite and ranks among the region's 'Big Four' dangerous species — what snake is it?
Russell's viper (Daboia russelii) is a species of highly venomous snake in the family Viperidae.
This interdisciplinary field studies signs and sign systems, breaking down into branches examining the formal relations between signs, their meanings, and their users — what's the field called?
Semiotics is the study of signs. It is an interdisciplinary field that examines what signs are, how they form sign systems, and how individuals use them to communicate meaning.
A white crystalline compound most important industrially as a nitrite salt, and probably best known as a food additive in processed meats. What is it?
Sodium nitrite is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula NaNO2.

Tracing its lineage back to ancestral fish from the Early Jurassic period roughly 174 to 201 million years ago, this family of 27 fish species is one of only two living branches of an ancient order that also includes the paddlefish — name this fish family?
Sturgeon are the 27 species of fish belonging to the family Acipenseridae.

Equal to one weber per square metre, this SI unit of magnetic flux density was adopted in 1960 and named for a Serbian-American electrical engineer, on the proposal of a Slovenian engineer — name this unit?
Tesla (unit) (symbol: T) is the unit of magnetic flux density (B) (also called magnetic B-field) in the International System of Units (SI).

This parasite can infect nearly any warm-blooded animal, but can only sexually reproduce inside cats, and is famous for altering infected rodents' behavior to make them less afraid of feline predators — what parasite is it?
Toxoplasma gondii is a species of parasitic alveolate that causes toxoplasmosis.
This NBC science fiction drama series ran for three seasons and 30 episodes between 2021 and 2024, receiving mixed reviews from critics. What show is it?
Vasculitis is a group of disorders that destroy blood vessels by inflammation.

This bird family, which also includes piculets, wrynecks, and sapsuckers, is absent from Australia and Madagascar, though one desert-dwelling member has adapted to drill into cacti — what family of birds is it?
Woodpecker are part of the bird family Picidae, which also includes the piculets, wrynecks, and sapsuckers.
Formed when acetic acid combines with a base, this ion is also nature's most common building block for biosynthesis — what is it?
Acetate: Salt formed from acetic acid and a base.
Also known as thymol seeds, bishop's weed, or carom, this Apiaceae herb's fruit is often mistaken for lovage seed — what is it?
Nicknamed the death cap, this deadly poisonous fungus resembles edible species like Caesar's mushroom and is native to Europe — what is it?
Amanita phalloides: Poisonous mushroom (death cap). The large fruiting bodies appear in summer and autumn; the caps are generally greenish in colour with a white stipe and gills.
Native to the eastern Mediterranean, this flowering herb's seeds taste similar to fennel, licorice, and tarragon and flavor candies and spirits — what is it?
Native to the northern tundra, this small mammal grows thick white fur for winter camouflage and forms monogamous breeding pairs while preying on lemmings and seabirds — what animal is it?
Arctic fox: Species of fox. It is well adapted to living in cold environments, and is known for its thick, warm fur that can be used as camouflage against snow in the winter.
This medical term describes the partial or complete wasting away of a body part due to poor nourishment, nerve loss, or disuse — what is the condition called?
Atrophy: Partial or complete wasting away of a part of the body. A diminished muscular trophic condition is designated as atrophy.
First flown in 1947 with a distinctive V-tail, this single-engine aircraft holds the record for the longest continuous production run in aviation history — which model?
Beechcraft Bonanza: Family of single engine American light aircraft, first flown in 1945.
Recognizable by its angled wings and forked tail, this scavenging bird of prey is thought to be the world's most abundant raptor, with a global population topping six million — which bird?
Black kite: Species of bird. The black kite or fire kite (Milvus migrans) is a medium-sized bird of prey in the family Accipitridae, which also includes many other diurnal raptors.
Named for the 18th-century French explorer who documented it on one of his expeditions, this thorny ornamental vine produces colorful bracts around three small waxy flowers — which plant is it?
First proposed after the 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese, this psychological theory says people are less likely to help a victim when others are present — what's it called?
Bystander effect: Social psychological theory. Recent research has focused on "real world" events captured on security cameras, and the coherency and robustness of the effect has come under question.

This polyatomic ion, CO3 with a 2- charge, is dissolved into water under pressure to make it fizzy, and also makes up much of the sedimentary rock in the Earth's crust — what's the ion (and salt) called?
Carbonate: Salt or ester of carbonic acid.
Discovered in 1945 and first sold in 1964, this class of beta-lactam antibiotics was originally pulled from a fungus once known as Cephalosporium — what's the family called?
Made in the skin after sun exposure and also known as vitamin D3, this compound is converted by the liver and kidneys into forms that help the body absorb calcium. What is it?

Cholecalciferol: Vitamin D3, a chemical compound. Cholecalciferol, also known as vitamin D3, colecalciferol or calciol, is a skin-made vitamin D that is found in certain foods and used as a dietary supplement.
First described by Linnaeus in 1758 and introduced to North America to control aphids, this red beetle with seven black spots gets its genus name from the Latin word for 'scarlet' — which species?
Coccinella septempunctata: Species of beetle. It inhabits many regions with a temperate climate.
This mathematical framework assigns one or more numbers to each point in space so its exact position can be pinned down — the foundation of analytic geometry. What is it called?
Coordinate system: Method for specifying point positions.

First described by Linnaeus in 1767, this citrus-family plant native to the Indian subcontinent has aromatic leaves essential to South Asian cooking, especially in India and Sri Lanka — which species?

Curry tree: Species of flowering plant. It is native to the Indian subcontinent, southern China and mainland Southeast Asia, and it has been introduced to other parts of southeast Asia and to Australia.
Nicknamed the 'gympie-gympie' by Queensland's Gubbi Gubbi people, this Australian and Malaysian rainforest plant delivers an infamously painful, long-lasting sting. What species is it?
Dendrocnide moroides: Species of plant in the nettle family.
A Canadian optical physicist at Waterloo, she shared the 2018 Nobel in Physics for the practical implementation of chirped pulse amplification — who is she?
Donna Strickland: Canadian physicist, engineer, and Nobel laureate.
Belonging to the order Anguilliformes and comprising roughly 1,000 species, these ray-finned predators transform dramatically from larva to adult and mostly live in salt water — what are they?
This fungal genus growing on rye and other cereals produces alkaloids that cause a poisoning condition in humans and livestock who eat contaminated grain — which group of fungi?
Ergot: Fungi of the genus Claviceps. The most prominent member of this group is Claviceps purpurea (rye ergot fungus).

Its mating has never once been observed in the wild, and its five life stages were once mistaken for five separate species — this critically endangered fish is threatened by dams and overfishing. What is it?
European eel: Species of fish. The five stages of their development were originally thought to be different species.
This genus of about 850 tropical tree, shrub, and vine species is best known for two cultivated fruit-bearing members and serves as a vital food source for wildlife across the tropics — which genus?
Ficus: Genus of flowering plants in the mulberry family Moraceae.
Native from the British Isles east to the Caucasus, this tree in the olive family is prized for wood that's flexible, strong, and lightweight — what is its scientific name?
Fraxinus excelsior: Species of deciduous tree.
Dubbed "the Godfather of AI" for his pioneering work on neural networks, this Nobel laureate quit Google in 2023 to warn about AI's risks. Who is he?
This waterfowl family member is smaller than a swan but larger than a duck; its young are called goslings, and a flock on the ground is known as a gaggle — what bird is it?
Goose: Common name for a group of waterfowl.
This Arabic word for a 'report' refers to the Islamic oral tradition of anecdotes preserving the words and deeds of Muhammad, ranking second only to the Quran in authority — what is it?
Hadith: Collections of sayings and teachings of Muhammad.
Often contracted from undercooked shellfish or contaminated water, this foodborne viral liver disease causes symptoms like jaundice and fever that typically last around eight weeks — what is it?
Hepatitis A: Acute infectious disease of the liver.
This hormone, produced by cells surrounding a growing embryo, is what's detected in pregnancy tests and sometimes secreted by tumors, aiding cancer diagnosis — what is it?
Human chorionic gonadotropin: Hormone for the maternal recognition of pregnancy.
Typically starting to work within an hour, this NSAID relieves pain, fever, and inflammation but can worsen asthma and, in later pregnancy, is considered harmful — which drug?

Credited with the oldest known systematic classification of chemical substances, this alchemist's corpus also contains the earliest instructions for deriving ammonium chloride from organic matter — who is he?
Jabir ibn Hayyan: Islamic alchemist and polymath (died c. 806–816)
Building his first firearm at age 13 in his father's gun shop, this American designer earned 128 patents and pioneered the autoloading pistol — who is he?
In this eye disorder, the cornea gradually thins and bulges into a cone shape, causing blurry or double vision often linked to excessive eye rubbing as a risk factor — which condition?
Keratoconus: Medical condition involving the eye.
This reddish-brown, bitter tincture dissolved opium poppy extract in alcohol and was once sold without a prescription as a cough and pain remedy — what is it?
Laudanum: Tincture of opium. Laudanum is a tincture of opium containing approximately 10% powdered opium by weight (the equivalent of 1% morphine).
Native to the Indo-Pacific, this venomous aquarium favorite sports red-and-black banded warning colors and ostentatious spiny fins, and has become an invasive nightmare in the Caribbean — what is it?
This flowering legume genus boasts over 199 species and has become such a successful invasive spreader in Iceland that it's now considered an ecological problem — which genus?
Dubbed "sea locusts" by the ancient Assyrians and "prawn killers" by others, these burrow-dwelling crustaceans are among the most important predators of shallow tropical seas. What are they?
Mantis shrimp: Order of crustaceans. Mantis shrimp are carnivorous marine crustaceans of the order Stomatopoda (from Ancient Greek στόμα (stóma) 'mouth' and πούς (poús) 'foot').
Made up of the dura, arachnoid, and pia mater, these three protective membranes shield the brain and spinal cord while containing cerebrospinal fluid — what are they called?
Meninges: Three membranes protecting the brain. In anatomy, the meninges (sing. meninx; from Ancient Greek μῆνινξ (mêninx) 'membrane') are protective membranes that cover the brain and spinal cord.
Developed for the Soviet Union, this swept-wing jet fighter dominated early dogfights in the Korean War and prompted the US to rush its F-86 Sabre into combat — which aircraft?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-15: Soviet fighter aircraft. The MiG-15 was one of the first successful jet fighters to incorporate swept wings to perform near Mach 1.

Prized by gourmet cooks yet toxic if eaten raw or undercooked, this genus of honeycomb-capped edible fungi is difficult to cultivate, making wild harvests a multimillion-dollar industry — which fungal genus?
Morchella: Genus of fungi. Morchella, the true morels, is a genus of edible sac fungi closely related to anatomically simpler cup fungi in the order Pezizales (division Ascomycota).
Sold under the brand name Deca-Durabolin, this anabolic steroid is prescribed for conditions like anemia and osteoporosis despite masculinizing side effects — which compound?
Nandrolone: Androgenic Anabolic steroid. Nandrolone, also known as 19-nortestosterone, is an endogenous androgen.
Humphry Davy coined this colorless gas's cheerful nickname for the euphoria it brings, and it still earns a spot on the WHO's Essential Medicines list for dentistry and surgery. What is it?
Nitrous oxide: Colourless non-flammable greenhouse gas.

A subdiscipline of metaphysics, this philosophical study of being asks what reality's most general features are, sorting things into particulars like Socrates and universals like the color green — what is it?
Ontology: Philosophical study of being. For example, social ontology examines basic concepts used in the social sciences.
This cat-family genus contains the five biggest living cats — jaguar, leopard, lion, snow leopard, and tiger — plus extinct relatives like the cave lion and American lion. Which genus is it?
This genus of fungi is responsible for both a groundbreaking antibiotic and the mold that ripens certain blue cheeses — which genus?
Whether captured chemically on light-sensitive film or electronically by an image sensor, this art is fundamentally the practice of recording light — what is it?
Photography: Art and practice of creating images by recording light.
Whether natural silk or synthetic nylon, this class of polymer is defined by repeating units joined through amide bonds — what is it?
Polyamide: Macromolecule with repeating units linked by amide bonds.
Genetic studies trace this most widely cultivated apricot species to Central Asia, though its scientific name nods to a country in the Caucasus — what is it?
Prunus armeniaca: Species of apricot. The native range is somewhat uncertain due to its extensive prehistoric cultivation.
About the size of a house cat, this nocturnal herbivorous marsupial thrives on Rottnest Island near Perth and is the only member of its genus — what is it?
Quokka: Small marsupial from southwestern Australia.

Covering more than 200 conditions from arthritis to soft-tissue pain syndromes, this umbrella term for chronic joint and connective-tissue pain gives its name to a whole medical specialty — what is it called?
Rheumatism: Medical conditions affecting the joints or connective tissue.
Known as rue or 'herb-of-grace,' this Mediterranean plant is prized for its bluish leaves and doubles as an insect repellent — which species?
Ruta graveolens: Species of plant. Ruta graveolens, commonly known as rue, common rue, ruda, arruda or herb-of-grace, is a species of the genus Ruta grown as an ornamental plant and herb.
This group of autoimmune diseases causes thickened skin and poor blood flow to the fingers and toes, with one form known as CREST syndrome — what is it called?
Scleroderma: Group of autoimmune diseases resulting in abnormal growth of connective tissue.
Also called herpes zoster, this viral disease paints a painful blistering rash down just one side of the body, and can leave lingering nerve pain called postherpetic neuralgia — what is it?
Shingles: Viral disease caused by the varicella zoster virus.

Known as sun spiders, camel spiders, or wind scorpions, this arachnid order is neither true spider nor scorpion, and urban legends wildly exaggerate its size, speed, and danger to humans — what is it?
Solifugae: Order of arachnids. The order includes more than 1,000 described species in about 147 genera.
Fired by Apple's board in 1985, he founded NeXT and bought a animation studio before returning a decade later to revolutionize consumer tech. Who?
Steve Jobs: American businessman and inventor (1955–2011)
